report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: The 2026 unified definition of acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) requires bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL and INR ≥1.5 before extrahepatic organ involvement is graded.
Many critically ill patients with cirrhosis have extrahepatic organ failure without such liver failure.
How the unified grade classifies them is unknown.
Methods.
We applied the unified, EASL-CLIF and NACSELD classifications around intensive care unit (ICU) admission to adults with cirrhosis in MIMIC-IV, excluding prior or perioperative liver transplantation.
The primary outcome was 28-day mortality; in-hospital mortality was examined in eICU.
Results.
Among 2,972 patients, 33.8% met ACLF criteria by the unified grade, 65.2% by EASL-CLIF and 29.9% by NACSELD.

Of EASL-CLIF-positive patients, 1,086 (56.0%) were assigned unified grade 0; 54.7% of them were ventilated, 48.7% received vasopressors, and their 28-day mortality was 32.6% (95% CI, 29.9% to 35.4%), versus 11.8% in patients negative by both definitions.
Patients with unified grade 0 accounted for 46.7% of all 28-day deaths.

The unified grade discriminated 28-day mortality less well than EASL-CLIF grade (difference in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], -0.071; 95% CI, -0.090 to -0.050) and the CLIF-C OF score (-0.105; -0.123 to -0.088).
Among 1,883 patients with coded decompensation, 45.8% of those EASL-CLIF-positive were assigned grade 0, with 28-day mortality of 34.3%.
In eICU, inhospital mortality was 28.9% among patients positive by EASL-CLIF alone.
In critically ill patients with cirrhosis, the unified grade assigned grade 0 to about half of those meeting EASL-CLIF criteria, and one in three of them died within 28 days.
In the ICU, unified grade 0 should not be read as low risk.
ACLF types A and B could not be determined.

Acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) is the name given to an abrupt deterioration of chronic liver disease that carries a high short-term risk of death, [1] but for more than a decade it has been defined in three different ways.

text.text: The Asian Pacific Association for the Study of the Liver (APASL) definition centers on jaundice and coagulopathy after an acute hepatic insult, followed by ascites or encephalopathy. [2] The European Association for the Study of the Liver-Chronic Liver Failure (EASL-CLIF) definition grades hepatic and extrahepatic organ failures in acutely decompensated cirrhosis and does not require liver failure. [3] The North American Consortium for the Study of End-Stage Liver Disease (NACSELD) definition requires at least two extrahepatic organ failures. [4, 5] The same patient can have ACLF under one definition and not under another, and the populations enrolled in studies, and their mortality, differ accordingly. [6, 7] In October 2026, five international liver societies agreed on a single definition. [8] ACLF now requires both a total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL and an international normalized ratio (INR) ≥1.5.

text.text: Severity is then graded by extrahepatic organ dysfunction or failure, and clinical types A and B are distinguished by the history of decompensation.

The definition draws on earlier consensus work on organ failure and on decompensation history. [9, 10, 11] Its central choice is that ACLF is a syndrome of liver failure: extrahepatic organ failure, however severe, does not qualify a patient who lacks it.

text.text: That choice has direct consequences in the intensive care unit (ICU).

Acute decompensation takes several clinical courses and has many precipitants, [12, 13] and the patients who reach intensive care commonly need a ventilator, vasopressors or renal support. [14, 15] Many of them are profoundly ill with a bilirubin well below 5 mg/dL.

text.text: When acutely decompensated, they have ACLF under EASL-CLIF criteria; under the unified definition they may not.

Studies in public ICU databases have so far used the earlier definitions, [16, 17, 18] and the first applications of the consensus and of related criteria come from hospitalized cohorts. [8, 19, 20] How the final grading rules classify critically ill patients with cirrhosis, and what the outcomes are for those who meet EASL-CLIF criteria but not the unified ones, has not been reported.

text.text: We applied the unified grade, the EASL-CLIF criteria and the NACSELD criteria to the same adults with cirrhosis around ICU admission in two intensive care databases.

We asked how many patients are classified differently, who they are, how often they die, and how well the unified grade separates survivors from non-survivors compared with existing grades and scores.

The primary cohort came from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) v3.1, which holds deidentified records of patients admitted to Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center from 2008 to 2022. [21, 22, 23] We included adults aged ≥18 years with a prespecified ICD-9-CM or ICD-10-CM code for cirrhosis (Supplementary Methods), informed by a published code set, [24] at their first recorded ICU stay, provided that bilirubin and INR were both measured between 24 hours before and 24 hours after ICU admission.

text.text: This observation window was used for all definitions and scores, and it closed at ICU discharge when that came first.

We excluded patients with a coded previous liver transplant and those whose transplant during the index admission was dated on or before the day of ICU admission, so that postoperative and posttransplant care was not graded as decompensated cirrhosis.
Patients transplanted later in the admission were retained.
The study is reported according to the STROBE and RECORD statements. [25, 26]

text.text: All definitions were implemented from structured data, and each component was scored from its worst value in the observation window.

We call our implementation of the consensus grading the unified grade. [8] Patients who met both hepatic thresholds (total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL and INR ≥1.5) were assigned grade 1 if they had extrahepatic organ dysfunction without failure, grade 2 if they had one extrahepatic organ failure, and grade 3 if they had two or more.

text.text: All other patients were assigned grade 0.

Kidney involvement was defined by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) stage, derived from the available creatinine and urine output measurements, and new renal replacement therapy (RRT), [27] circulatory involvement by mean arterial pressure and vasopressor use, and respiratory involvement by oxygenation and invasive mechanical ventilation.

text.text: West Haven grade is not recorded in either database.

We therefore used the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) as a proxy. [28, 29] Cerebral failure was defined as a score ≤13, as in earlier ICU database studies, [16, 17, 18] and cerebral dysfunction as a score of 14, a rule set for this study.

EASL-CLIF grade, the CLIF Consortium Organ Failure (CLIF-C OF) score, NACSELD ACLF, MELD 3.0, MELD-Na and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score were calculated from the same data. [3, 5, 30, 31, 32, 33] Nonhepatic components that were not measured were scored as normal.

text.text: The unified and EASL-CLIF classifications were analyzed both as four-level grades and as present or absent.
The principal diagnosis of the hospitalization, grouped into ten categories, served as a proxy for the reason for admission.
Thresholds, variable mappings and code lists are given in the Supplementary Methods.
The primary outcome was death from any cause within 28 days of ICU admission.
Secondary outcomes were death within 90 days and death during the index hospitalization.
Deaths were ascertained from hospital records and linked state death records; MIMIC-IV censors dates of death more than one year after the last hospital discharge. [22]

text.text: We report the proportion of patients meeting each definition and the cross-classification of unified and EASL-CLIF grades.

Patients were then divided into four groups according to whether they were positive by both classifications, by one, or by neither, and clinical characteristics and mortality were compared across these groups.
For each definition we also calculated the proportion of all deaths that occurred in patients it classified as not having ACLF.

Proportions are given with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs), [34] survival was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method, and the trend in mortality across grades was tested by logistic regression with grade as an ordinal term.

[36] Calibration of the continuous scores was assessed after fivefold cross-fitted logistic mapping. [37] The comparisons are unadjusted, because the aim was to compare the classifications as they would be used.

Two analyses tested whether the results depended on how respiratory failure was counted: in one, invasive ventilation alone no longer qualified as respiratory failure under either definition, so that impaired oxygenation was required; in the other, the cohort was restricted to patients not intubated at ICU admission.
Two analyses addressed the cerebral criterion, by excluding patients sedated or intubated at admission and by omitting the cerebral domain.

Three addressed transplantation: a composite outcome of death or liver transplantation by day 28, exclusion of all index-admission transplants and transplant status codes, and removal of the transplant exclusions altogether.

The remaining analyses excluded elective admissions, used only the first 24 or 48 hours after admission, or were restricted to patients with all components measured or to those alive and in the ICU at 24 hours (Table 3).

text.text: Because the EASL-CLIF definition applies to acutely decompensated cirrhosis, a post hoc analysis restricted the cohort to patients with a diagnosis code for ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, esophageal variceal bleeding, hepatorenal syndrome, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or jaundice during the index hospitalization, and then also excluded those whose principal diagnosis was cardiovascular, postoperative or neoplastic.
Prespecified subgroups were alcohol-related cirrhosis, infection at admission and intubation at admission.

In the eICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU-CRD) v2.0, a multicenter ICU database, [38, 39] we applied the same observation window, the same requirement for bilirubin and INR, and the same scoring rules. eICU has no follow-up after discharge, so the endpoint was in-hospital mortality.

text.text: A complete-case analysis, limited to patients with a cirrhosis code linked to the index ICU stay, is reported as a sensitivity analysis.
Of 3,806 adults with coded cirrhosis at their first ICU stay, 3,232 had both bilirubin and INR measured in the observation window.
We excluded 260 with a coded previous transplant or a transplant dated on or before the day of ICU admission, which left 2,972 patients; 67 of them were transplanted later in the admission.
The median age was 59 years, 36.3% were women and 56.5% had alcohol-related cirrhosis (Table 1).

text.text: The median bilirubin was 3.2 mg/dL and the median SOFA score was 7.
There were 980 deaths (33.0%) by day 28, 1,255 by day 90 and 849 during the index hospitalization.

ACLF criteria were met by 33.8% of patients (95% CI, 32.1% to 35.5%) under the unified grade, 65.2% (63.5% to 66.9%) under EASL-CLIF and 29.9% (28.3% to 31.6%) under NACSELD.
The unified grade and EASL-CLIF disagreed in 1,238 patients, and almost always in one direction: 1,086 were positive by EASL-CLIF alone and 152 by the unified grade alone (Fig. 1).

text.text: The 1,086 made up 56.0% of all EASL-CLIF-positive patients.
They included 305 patients with EASL-CLIF grade 3, the most severe grade, whose 28-day mortality was 48.5%.
These 1,086 patients had little biochemical liver failure and a great deal of organ support (Table 2).
text.formatted: These 1,086 patients had little biochemical liver failure and a great deal of organ support (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Their median bilirubin was 1.9 mg/dL and their median INR 1.7; 1,067 fell below one or both hepatic thresholds, and the other 19 met both but had no qualifying extrahepatic finding under the unified grade.
Yet 54.7% received invasive mechanical ventilation, 48.7% received vasopressors and 6.6% received RRT.
By EASL-CLIF criteria, 61.8% had respiratory failure, 52.5% kidney failure and 48.7% circulatory failure.
Their median SOFA score was 8 and their median MELD 3.0 was 24, between the values in patients negative by both definitions (4 and 16) and in patients positive by both (11 and 36).

text.text: Infection or sepsis was the most frequent named principal diagnosis (24.0%), followed by liver-related diagnoses (17.9%); 23.5% fell in the residual category.
Their 28-day mortality was 32.6% (95% CI, 29.9% to 35.4%).

This was nearly three times the mortality of patients negative by both definitions (11.8%; 9.8% to 14.1%) and higher than that of the 152 patients positive by the unified grade alone (21.7%; 15.9% to 28.9%).
Patients positive by both definitions had the highest mortality, 57.4%.
By 90 days, 42.9% of the patients positive by EASL-CLIF alone had died.

Mortality rose with unified grade.
At 28 days it was 23.3%, 29.2%, 43.8% and 65.6% for grades 0 to 3, and at 90 days 32.2%, 42.6%, 54.8% and 73.4% (Fig. 2 and Table S2).

text.text: The gradient was steep above grade 0.

Grade 0 itself, however, held two thirds of the cohort (1,968 patients) and combined two very different groups: the 882 patients negative by both definitions and the 1,086 positive by EASL-CLIF alone.
The unified grade discriminated 28-day mortality less well than EASL-CLIF grade and the CLIF-C OF score.

Its AUC was 0.665 (95% CI, 0.646 to 0.684), against 0.736 for EASL-CLIF grade and 0.771 for the CLIF-C OF score; the paired differences were -0.071 (-0.090 to -0.050) and -0.105 (-0.123 to -0.088) (Fig. 3).

The reclassified group remained when ventilation alone no longer counted as respiratory failure.
With impaired oxygenation required, 59.9% of patients were EASL-CLIF-positive, 957 were positive by EASL-CLIF alone, and their 28-day mortality was 34.9%.
Among the 2,308 patients not intubated at ICU admission, 61.0% were EASL-CLIF-positive, 763 were positive by EASL-CLIF alone, and their mortality was 31.7%.
The handling of transplantation changed little.

Overall 28-day mortality was 33.7% when all indexadmission transplants and transplant status codes were excluded and 30.4% when no transplant exclusion was applied, and the composite of death or transplantation by day 28 occurred in 1,033 patients (34.8%); reclassification and discrimination were close to the main analysis in each case (Table S13), as they were after exclusion of elective admissions.

text.text: Of 1,346 EASL-CLIF-positive patients in this subgroup, 616 (45.8%) were assigned unified grade 0.
Their 28-day mortality was 34.3% (95% CI, 30.6% to 38.1%), and unified grade 0 accounted for 37.8% of 28-day deaths.
When patients with a cardiovascular, postoperative or neoplastic principal diagnosis were also excluded (n=1,665), the corresponding values were 43.2%, 33.3% (29.4% to 37.5%) and 34.1%.
In both subgroups the unified grade discriminated less well than EASL-CLIF grade (differences in AUC, -0.051 [-0.076 to -0.027] and -0.047 [-0.073 to -0.021]).
The difference in AUC between the unified grade and both comparators was negative in every sensitivity analysis (Table 3).

MIMIC-IV uses 28-day mortality and eICU uses inhospital mortality.
In adults with cirrhosis admitted to intensive care, the unified ACLF grade classified about half as many patients as having ACLF as the EASL-CLIF criteria did.
The patients who made up the difference were not mildly ill.
About half were ventilated, about half received vasopressors, and one in three died within 28 days.
They accounted for most of the deaths at grade 0, where nearly half of all 28-day deaths occurred, and the unified grade discriminated mortality less well than EASL-CLIF grade or the CLIF-C OF score.
Among patients with coded decompensation the reclassified share was somewhat smaller, 45.8% of those EASL-CLIF-positive, and their mortality was similar.
Reclassification in the same direction was seen in eICU, among 1,008 patients from 139 hospitals, with in-hospital mortality as the endpoint.
This is what the definition was designed to do, applied to a population in which extrahepatic organ failure is common.

The consensus requires both hepatic thresholds for ACLF and grades severity by extrahepatic dysfunction or failure. [8] Patients with cirrhosis in the ICU, however, often need support for an organ other than the liver while their bilirubin is only modestly raised: the median was 3.2 mg/dL in our cohort and 1.9 mg/dL in the patients positive by EASL-CLIF alone.

text.text: EASL-CLIF counts such patients as ACLF on the strength of their extrahepatic organ failure.
The unified definition does not.

The group was not created by counting every ventilated patient as having respiratory failure: it still made up about a third of the cohort, with 28-day mortality of 34.9% and 31.7%, when impaired oxygenation was required and when patients intubated at admission were excluded.
Whether these patients have ACLF is a question of definition that outcome data cannot settle.
What the data show is that, in the ICU, the absence of unified ACLF says little about risk.
Mortality at grade 0 ranged from 11.8% in patients negative by both definitions to 32.6% in those positive by EASL-CLIF alone, and grade 0 held two thirds of the cohort.
This heterogeneity is a likely reason why the grade discriminated less well than EASL-CLIF grade even though its mortality gradient above grade 0 was steep.

Earlier ICU studies used the established ACLF frameworks to characterize organ failure or to compare prognostic scores. [16, 17, 18, 40] In broader cirrhosis cohorts, definitions that turn on a biochemical liver threshold are known to select different patients from those based on organ failure, most recently in a comparison of criteria based on the 2025 consensus with A-TANGO. [6, 20, 41] The consensus document reports first applications in international cohorts, and a conference report applied a precursor with different INR and blood-pressure rules. [8, 19] To our knowledge, the final grading rules have not previously been reported in a dedicated intensive care cohort.

text.text: Applied there to the same patients as two established definitions, they leave about half of the EASL-CLIF population outside ACLF.
Three practical points follow.
First, for the intensivist and the hepatologist at the bedside, unified grade 0 is not reassurance.

In the reclassified group, about half of the patients were ventilated, about half received vasopressors and the median bilirubin was 1.9 mg/dL; none of them is classified as ACLF by the unified grade, and one in three died within a month.

Current guidance already bases prognosis in critically ill patients with cirrhosis on hepatic and extrahepatic organ failure, [42] and our findings show why this should not change when the unified grade is 0.
text.formatted: Current guidance already bases prognosis in critically ill patients with cirrhosis on hepatic and extrahepatic organ failure, <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[42]</ref> and our findings show why this should not change when the unified grade is 0.

text.text: Second, the unified grade and EASL-CLIF used as entry criteria would enroll ICU populations with different risks, and about half of the ICU patients who meet EASL-CLIF criteria would be ineligible under the unified grade.

Studies that adopt the unified definition in critical care should report the patients below the hepatic thresholds alongside those with ACLF, so that this group does not drop out of the literature when the definition changes.
Third, the group needs to be described in its own terms.
Critically ill patients with cirrhosis who have extrahepatic organ failure without liver failure are numerous and at high risk.
Whether they are best served by pathways built for ACLF, including early transplant evaluation, or by general critical care is a question that the new definition makes visible and does not answer.
Several limitations bear on interpretation.
The cohort was defined by a diagnosis code for cirrhosis, whereas the EASL-CLIF definition applies to acute decompensation.

Restriction to patients with coded decompensation lowered the reclassified share from 56.0% to 45.8% with similar mortality, but hospital codes cannot show that decompensation was acute or preceded ICU admission.
We also graded patients from structured records.

The history of decompensation is not available, so types A and B could not be assigned and our findings concern grading only. [8] West Haven grade was replaced by the GCS, which can register sedation or non-hepatic coma as cerebral failure, [18, 29] and the indications for ventilation and vasopressors could not be adjudicated.

text.text: The direction of the results was unchanged when sedated or intubated patients were excluded, when the cerebral domain was omitted and when respiratory failure required impaired oxygenation, but circulatory failure could not be examined in this way.

Classification from structured data can also differ from classification by chart review. [43] Unmeasured components were scored as normal, which can understate organ involvement under every definition.

text.text: In the 447 patients with all components measured the unified grade still had the lower AUC, but its difference from EASL-CLIF grade was small and imprecise.
Grades used the worst values up to 24 hours after admission, so they describe risk once the first day's data are available, not at the moment of admission.
The primary cohort came from one center. eICU showed the same direction of reclassification among patients from 139 hospitals, with in-hospital mortality as its only endpoint.
Cirrhosis was identified from diagnosis codes, and deaths after discharge may be incompletely captured in MIMIC-IV, which would lower 28-day and 90-day mortality in all groups.
Finally, a four-level grade cannot order risk as finely as a score with many values; the comparison with EASL-CLIF grade, which also has four levels, is the fairer one, and it pointed the same way.

In critically ill patients with cirrhosis, the unified ACLF grade assigned grade 0 to about half of those meeting EASL-CLIF criteria (56.0% overall and 45.8% of those with coded decompensation), and one in three of these patients died within 28 days.
In the ICU, unified grade 0 does not indicate low risk, and extrahepatic organ failure should be assessed and reported alongside it.
These findings concern the grading component; ACLF types A and B could not be determined.
